name: Tahitian Tamau (Ground Beat)
desc: The tamau is the unbroken ground pulse that underpins every Tahitian otea: the low sharkskin pahu (tariparau) marks the quarter beats while the high toere slit-drum lays a steady running ostinato of eighths over it. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Napoko
desc: Napoko is one of the named toere phrases (pehe) pieced together to build an otea; its syncopated short-short-long cell repeats over the pahu half-bar pulse, the high toere ostinato cuing dancers. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Toma (Cadence)
desc: The toma is the closing pattern of a pehe: it signals tempo changes and choreographic cues to the dancers, the toere driving toward a marked cadence over the steady pahu. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Pahae
desc: Pahae is a flexible toere phrase in the Tahitian percussion vocabulary, its broken-triplet feel filling the spaces of the ground beat; assembled like a word into the otea 'sentence'. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Paea
desc: Paea is a named toere ostinato accenting the and-of-each-beat to create a galloping cross-rhythm against the pahu quarters, a staple cell in Heiva otea repertoire. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Puara-Ta
desc: Puara-ta is a dense toere phrase from the named pehe vocabulary, packing four-stroke runs that contribute to the 'thick river of notes' when split across players. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Takoto
desc: Takoto ('to lie down') is a sparser named toere cell that opens space in the texture, often used as a contrasting part so a second group of drummers can fill the gaps. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Mati
desc: Mati is a named toere phrase built on paired strokes at the head of each beat, a bright clipped motif used to lock a section together over the pahu pulse. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Bora Bora
desc: The 'Bora Bora' pehe is a regional named toere phrase in the Tahitian vocabulary, an off-beat-leaning ostinato evoking the Leeward-island style. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Fa'arapu
desc: Fa'arapu is the fast continuous toere roll that accompanies the rapid circular hip-shaking figure of the same name; an unbroken stream of sixteenths over the pahu, signalling the dancers to whirl. Bass = pahu, snareAccent = toere.

name: Tahitian Otea Part A / Part B Interlock
desc: In a full otea, one group of toere plays Part A on the beats while a second group fills the off-beats (Part B), so eight one-handed players sound like a single woody drum-roll. Bass = pahu ground, snareAccent = combined toere stream.

name: Cook Islands Ura Pa'u Drum Dance
desc: The ura pa'u is the fast Cook Islands drum dance: the deep pate/pa'u skin drum lays the heartbeat while interlocking tokere slit-drums drive the dancers' rapid hip rotations to a dramatic finish. Bass = pa'u, snareAccent = tokere.

name: Cook Islands Tokere Interlock (Tini Ka'ara)
desc: In a tini ka'ara ensemble three sizes of tokere (taki, tangarongaro, mamaiti) interlock at different pitches above the pate; their rhythms directly direct dancers' body and hand movements. Bass = pate, snareAccent = high tokere.

name: Cook Islands Pate Fast Roll
desc: A driving fast pate roll typical of Cook Islands drum dance climaxes: a continuous high slit-drum stream over a half-bar pa'u pulse, used as the actions of the dancers grow short and rapid. Bass = pa'u, snareAccent = pate.

name: Samoan Pate-Lali Interlock
desc: The classic Samoan two-drum interlock: the large logo/lali sounds the loud, strong stroke on beat 1 while the higher, weaker pate answers on beat 3, framing siva song and dance. Bass = lali, snareAccent = pate.

name: Samoan Pate Fast Ostinato
desc: A fast pate ostinato made from a single hollowed Miro-wood log drum, its loud distinctive crack carrying the pulse for siva and group dances. Bass = lali, snareAccent = pate.

name: Samoan Fa'ataupati (Slap Dance)
desc: The fa'ataupati is the male Samoan slap dance born from swatting mosquitoes: forceful hand-slaps on chest, thighs and arms create a syncopated body-percussion rhythm with stamped accents. Bass = thigh/floor stamp, snareAccent = body slap.

name: Samoan Sasa
desc: Sasa ('to strike') is the seated/standing group dance whose unison hand-claps and strikes to body and floor are driven by the pate; rapid synchronized accents symbolise community cooperation. Bass = lali, snareAccent = clap/strike with pate.

name: Samoan Ma'ulu'ulu
desc: Ma'ulu'ulu is a gentle seated narrative dance: performers sit cross-legged, rock the torso and illustrate the sung text with finger and arm gestures over a calm pate pulse. Bass = lali, snareAccent = pate.

name: Samoan Lali Tatasi-Talua
desc: Lali are played in pairs: one drummer beats the larger Tatasi on the strong beats while the second plays the smaller lali in the answering pattern called Talua, traditionally used to call and announce. Bass = Tatasi (large lali), snareAccent = Talua (small lali).

name: Tongan Nafa Lakalaka
desc: One to five nafa drums of different sizes, struck with soft-headed sticks, lay the measured beat for the lakalaka and ma'ulu'ulu sung dances; large drum on the beat, smaller on the off-beat. Bass = large nafa, snareAccent = small nafa.

name: Tongan Me'etu'upaki (Paddle Dance)
desc: In the ancient me'etu'upaki paddle-club dance the dance master beats a small lali slit-drum to keep time while dancers sing; the tempo starts slow and accelerates toward the climax. Bass = lali, snareAccent = quickening pulse.

name: Tongan Lali Signal Call
desc: The lali, gouged from a hardwood log (the bigger the branch, the deeper the tone), beats a rolling call traditionally used to summon villagers and announce ceremonies. Bass = large lali, snareAccent = small lali.

name: Maori Haka Stamp & Slap
desc: The haka is declaimed in triple metre with heavy foot-stamping (waewae takahia) and rhythmic slaps to chest, thighs and arms creating built-in percussion under the chanted, called-and-response leader's voice. Bass = foot stamp, snareAccent = body slap.

name: Maori Poi Strike Rhythm
desc: In poi the swung ball is struck against the hand or body to punctuate direction changes; the percussive thwack is an integral compositional element over a steady danceable pulse for waiata-a-ringa. Bass = ground pulse, snareAccent = poi strike.

name: Maori Pate (Slit Drum)
desc: The pate, a small wooden slit drum, was struck to keep an interlocking pulse in some Maori and wider Polynesian performance; bright high strokes punctuate the song's beat. Bass = pulse, snareAccent = pate.

name: Hawaiian Ipu Heke (Hula Kahiko)
desc: The ho'opa'a strikes the double-gourd ipu heke to a steady chant: a deep thump (gourd on the mat) on the beat answered by lighter finger slaps on the off-beats, marking time for hula kahiko. Bass = ipu thump, snareAccent = finger slap.

name: Hawaiian Pahu (Sharkskin Drum)
desc: The sacred pahu, carved from a coconut trunk with a sharkskin head, is played with palms and fingers; its measured beat guides hula dancers and dictates the pace of the sacred kahiko. Bass = open palm tone, snareAccent = rim/finger slap.

name: Hawaiian Pu'ili & 'Uli'uli
desc: Split-bamboo pu'ili rattle-sticks struck on the body and partners, and the gourd-and-feather 'uli'uli shaken to the chant, add a continuous rustling eighth-note layer over the ipu pulse in hula. Bass = ipu pulse, snareAccent = pu'ili/'uli'uli strike.

name: Fijian Derua Stamping Tubes
desc: Derua, hollow bamboo tubes stamped on mats or the earth, create deep resonant polyrhythms that guide every movement of the Fijian meke; differing tube lengths give differing pitches. Bass = long derua, snareAccent = short derua.

name: Fijian Lali & Cobo (Meke)
desc: In the meke the hardwood lali drum lays the foundation while cobo, cupped rhythmic hand-clapping by the seated chorus, fills a continuous off-beat layer to drive the danced storytelling. Bass = lali, snareAccent = cobo clap.

name: PNG Kundu Hourglass Drum
desc: The kundu, an hourglass hand-drum with a lizard- or possum-skin head, is carried and beaten in unison by rows of dancers to drive the singsing; its galloping pulse paces the chanted dance. Bass = open belly tone, snareAccent = edge strike.

name: PNG Garamut Signal Rhythm
desc: The garamut, a log slit-gong struck near the slit and on the sides, beats clan-specific patterns that carry messages for kilometres and also rhythm the singsing; struck with one or two sticks. Bass = side/low strike, snareAccent = slit/high strike.

name: Solomon Islands 'Au Paina Panpipe Ensemble
desc: The 'au paina is one of the prestigious 'Are'are bamboo panpipe ensembles of Malaita, performed only for major ancestor-cult festivals; players hocket interlocking pipe figures over a stamped pulse. Bass = bass pipes, snareAccent = upper interlocking pipes.

name: Solomon Islands Bamboo Band Stomp
desc: Solomon Islands bamboo bands strike tuned open-ended bamboo tubes with rubber sandals, the deep bass tubes on the beat and shorter tubes filling between, a festival sound of the islands. Bass = long bass tube, snareAccent = short tube.

name: Aboriginal Bilma Clapsticks (Wangga)
desc: Bilma (bimli) clapsticks keep a precise even beat accompanying the didgeridoo in Yolngu ceremony; in the Wangga genre the song-man introduces the sticks over the drone, the pattern handed down for generations. Bass = didgeridoo accent, snareAccent = clapstick.

name: Aboriginal Fast Clapstick Ostinato (Corroboree)
desc: In fast corroboree songs the clapsticks drive a rapid continuous ostinato locked to the didgeridoo's fast-tongued rhythmic drone, maintaining the chant's tempo for the dancers. Bass = didgeridoo pulse, snareAccent = fast clapsticks.
